Narragansett

Narragansett Indian Tribe publications connect seasonal community life, survival through state interference, later institutions and cultural-resource protection. This starting path retains the Tribe’s perspective while keeping unverified archaeological ages, present totals and legal conclusions separate.

01

Identity and context

The Narragansett Indian Tribe has enduring relationships with Rhode Island and southern New England.

Read the sources [1] Narragansett Indian Tribe

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Narragansett-authored history, language, land and sovereignty. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Narragansett Indian Tribe [2] narragansetthistoricalsociety.com [3] narragansettri.gov

03

Seasonal community life and colonial violence

The Tribe’s early-history account describes seasonal movement between winter homes and shore settings and recalls the violence of the Great Swamp Massacre in 1675. It presents community history from a Narragansett perspective. Numerical capacity estimates, claims about other peoples’ historical obligations and precise archaeological ages are not used to determine present identities or boundaries.

Read the sources [1] Narragansett Indian Tribe

04

Meetings and institutions across disruption

The perseverance account explains that community members continued recognizing leaders and holding meetings despite state efforts to dismantle tribal institutions. It later describes organizing, publishing The Narragansett Dawn and building a Longhouse in the1940s. The earlier Indian Meeting House also appears as a community meeting place. Original minutes, magazine issues and land records remain to inspect.

Read the sources [4] Narragansett Indian Tribe

05

Cultural places as finite resources

The historic-preservation office explains that excavation and construction can irreversibly alter cultural places. Its public account describes consultation and performance standards intended to protect them. These are stated responsibilities and concerns, not an invitation to investigate sensitive sites or a legal assessment of a particular project.

Read the sources [5] Narragansett Indian Tribe

Early History — Narragansett community account ↗

The Tribe’s historical perspective describes seasonal community life and the violence of King Philip’s War. Its account should be read with original colonial records and community scholarship still to inspect.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete Early History body after the heading, with synthesis confined to seasonal home/shore activity and the 1675 Great Swamp Massacre/dispersion paragraphs. Age-of-occupation estimates, tributary lists and first-contact superlatives excluded.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Normal public HTTP 200 body read. No archaeological report, colonial journal, treaty, casualty list or village evidence inspected. The page’s30, 000-year statement, numerical household/canoe capacity, legal land-use claims and current affiliation inferences are not adopted.

Preservation — Narragansett Indian Tribal Historic Preservation Office ↗

The office explains why archaeological places are finite cultural resources and how consultation and performance standards can protect them. The public programme description does not authorize access to sensitive sites.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete NITHPO and Archaeological Administration main prose, web-reader lines108–115, before repeated Save/footer text.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Normal public HTTP 200 body read. No site inventories, ancestral remains, archaeological excavations, consultation files or legal instruments inspected.
